Stahlgewitter - The honour of Stedingen (Click CC for English Subs)

The following song is about the final battle of the people of Stedingen against the Christian crusaders in 1234.

The people of Stedingen (a Frisian tribe of Germanic origin native to the coastal parts of the Netherlands and Germany) were able to resist against the superiority in manpower and armament of the Christian military for quite a long time (1204-1234), they refused to give up their Pagan traditions and their independence. They withstood the harassment of the Archbishop of Bremen Gerhard I but were finally defeated by an army of crusaders under Archbishop of Bremen Gerhard II.

Just for the understanding of some terms used in this song:

An Irminsul is a kind of pillar which played an important role in Germanic paganism. Those pillars were handcrafted figures of trees and often portrayed the world tree which is also an object of worship in other Indo-European religions. There are also Germanic pillars which symbolize Germanic gods but unlike in the Slavonic religion they were not as popular as their "tree-counterparts".

Wooden horse heads were used as a decoration of the gables. It is said that the use of a portray of a horse head goes back to the eight-legged horse of Odin, Sleipnir. The practical use of horse-headed side boards lies in the increased air/storm resistance of the roof.

In the upper right corner you can see a picture of the Hartwarder Friese, this memorial was constructed to remember the fight for freedom of the Stedinger people. It holds an inscription with the slogan "Liewer düd aß Slaawe" which translated from Low German means "Better dead than a slave".

The elected (by thing) military leaders of the Stedinger were Bolko von Bardenfleth, Detmar tom Dyk and Thammo von Huntorp.

A thing was the governing assembly of Germanic societies, made up of the free people of the community presided over by lawspeakers. Its meeting-place was called a thingstead.﻿
